teaser: She was queen for nine days. He painted her last two minutes.
review_notes:
Jane Grey: proclaimed queen July 1553, executed 12 February 1554 at the Tower, aged about 16 or 17; executed outdoors on Tower Green.
Her reported words while groping for the block (“What shall I do? Where is it?”) come from a contemporary account.
Man guiding her identified as Sir John Brydges, Lieutenant of the Tower.
Painting believed destroyed in the 1928 Thames flood at the Tate, found rolled up in 1973 by curator Christopher Johnson; bequeathed by Lord Cheylesmore 1902; first bought by Anatole Demidoff.
Dimensions 246 x 297 cm.
The seated lady holding Jane's discarded gown and jewels in her lap: check against National Gallery description.
Delaroche's use of small wax figures to plan compositions.
“From today, painting is dead” is presented as a legend.

lesson.text: Nine days. That is how long Lady Jane Grey was queen of England in July 1553. She was sixteen or seventeen, a studious Protestant girl pushed onto the throne by ambitious relatives. Then her Catholic cousin Mary took the crown, and Jane went to the Tower of London.

Seven months later, on February 12, 1554, she was beheaded. Almost three centuries after that, in Paris, Paul Delaroche chose to paint not the blow of the axe but the two minutes before it. Nothing violent has happened yet. That is exactly why the picture is hard to bear.

The canvas is enormous: about 2.5 meters high and 3 meters wide (roughly 8 by 10 feet). The figures are life-size and stand on a platform at the level of your own feet. In a gallery, you are not looking at a scene. You are standing in the front row.

lesson.title: Five people, five reactions
lesson.text: Start with the people. Each one handles the moment differently.

spots.title: Jane
spots.text: Blindfolded, lips slightly parted, skin as pale as her dress. Delaroche gives her no visible fear, only a kind of lost concentration.

spots.title: The lieutenant
spots.text: An older man in a fur-lined coat bends over her and steers her gently. He is usually identified as the officer in charge of the Tower. He looks like a father helping a child.

spots.title: The two ladies
spots.text: One has collapsed against the pillar, eyes shut. The other has turned to the wall with her hands above her head. Neither can watch, which tells you what is coming.

spots.title: The executioner
spots.text: He waits, weight on one leg, eyes lowered. Delaroche makes him patient and almost sorry, not a monster. A man about to do a job.

lesson.text: Delaroche paints the moment before the event. The viewer's imagination finishes the scene, and that is far stronger than showing it.

The detail that struck people most in 1834, when the picture was first shown at the Paris Salon, the big official exhibition, comes from an eyewitness account. Once the blindfold was tied, Jane could not find the block. She is said to have cried out, asking where it was.
Delaroche builds the whole picture around that groping gesture.

lines.label: The reaching arm
lines.text: Her arm stretches down and forward, fingers spread in the air. A few centimeters below them stands the wooden block she cannot see.

lines.label: The helping curve
lines.text: The lieutenant's body arches over her like a bracket and ends in his hand on her forearm. He is guiding her toward her own death, as kindly as he can.

lines.label: The upright
lines.text: The executioner is the only straight vertical among bending, sinking figures. He is the fixed point everything else is falling toward.

lesson.text: Every curved line in the picture bends toward the center, and the center is a girl in white. That dress is the brightest thing on the canvas by far. The rest is brown, black and dull red, like a stage with a single spotlight.

The white satin is an invention. Accounts of the day say Jane wore black, and she was executed in the open air, on a green inside the Tower, not in a dim stone hall. Delaroche moved the scene indoors because darkness made a better theater.

Theater is the right word. Delaroche loved the stage and is said to have planned his pictures with small wax figures arranged in a box, like a director blocking a scene. The shallow platform, the backdrop of carved arches, the actors lined up left to right: all of it could be a play frozen at its climax.
He also dressed the set with props, and each prop carries a piece of the story. One of them is easy to overlook because it sits in a lap, far from the action.
Before kneeling, Jane handed over her dress and her jewels. Who is holding them?

spots.title: The fainting lady's lap
spots.text: The seated lady has Jane's outer gown spread over her knees, with strings of pearls and a necklace lying in the folds. The queen has already been stripped of everything that made her one.

lesson.text: With her finery gone, Jane kneels in what is basically her underclothes: a satin petticoat and a laced bodice. The costume turns a political prisoner into something simpler and more shocking for the public of 1834, a defenseless young girl.

French viewers saw their own history in this English one. Many in the Salon crowd had parents who remembered the guillotine, and a queen led to the scaffold recalled Marie Antoinette. The Revolution of 1830 had happened only four years earlier.

The picture was the hit of the Salon. People crowded in front of it, and engravings carried the image across Europe. A Russian millionaire, Anatole Demidoff, owned it. It later went to England, and in 1902 it was left to the nation. Then it vanished.

In 1928 the River Thames flooded the basement of the Tate Gallery, where the canvas was stored. It was written off as destroyed. In 1973 a curator searching for another lost picture unrolled a damaged canvas and found Lady Jane Grey inside, almost unharmed.

During those 45 missing years, Delaroche's reputation had also sunk. His glassy, storytelling style was everything modern art rejected. When the National Gallery hung the rediscovered picture in 1975, experts expected a curiosity. Visitors made it one of the most visited paintings in the building.

spots.title: The block
spots.text: Low, heavy, with an iron ring to chain it down. Delaroche puts it at the very front and center, closer to you than any person in the picture.

spots.title: The straw
spots.text: Clean yellow straw spread around the block. Its purpose is to soak up blood. This is the most brutal object in the painting, and the brightest after the dress.

spots.title: The cushion
spots.text: A green velvet cushion with gold tassels waits for her knees. A last courtesy owed to rank, absurd and touching next to the straw.

spots.title: The axe
spots.text: The blade rests on the floor, clean and dull gray, held as casually as a walking stick. It points nowhere yet.

spots.title: Rope and knife
spots.text: At the executioner's belt hang a coil of rope and a knife, the backup tools of his trade.

spots.title: The blindfold
spots.text: A plain white cloth knotted behind the head, with a lock of red-gold hair falling over her shoulder. Her hair is loose so the neck can be bared.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: Her right hand hangs open, fingers spread, searching the air to her side. Both hands are lost at once.

spots.title: Hands on the wall
spots.text: The standing lady presses her wrists against the stone column. We never see her face, and we do not need to.

lesson.text: Delaroche is often quoted as saying, on first seeing a photograph around 1839, “From today, painting is dead.” There is no solid proof he said it. What is certain is that his own way of painting, sharp, staged and full of true-looking detail, is close to what cinema would later do.

That may be the best way to stand in front of this canvas. Think of it as a still from a historical film made sixty years before film existed: costume, lighting, casting, and a director who knows that the audience is most afraid just before the cut.

quiz.question: How long was Lady Jane Grey queen of England?
quiz.explanation: She reigned for nine days in July 1553.

quiz.question: Which moment did Delaroche choose to paint?
options: The minutes just before the execution
quiz.explanation: Nothing violent has happened yet, and the viewer imagines the rest.

quiz.question: What is the straw around the block for?
quiz.explanation: It is spread there to absorb the blood.

quiz.question: What did Delaroche change compared with the historical accounts?
options: He moved the scene indoors and dressed her in white
quiz.explanation: She reportedly wore black and died outdoors on a green inside the Tower.

quiz.question: What happened to the painting in 1928?
options: It was stolen from the Louvre
It was sold to a Russian collector
It was believed destroyed in a flood
quiz.explanation: The Thames flooded the Tate's basement and the canvas was written off until 1973.

quiz.question: Where are Jane's dress and jewels in the picture?
options: In the lap of the seated lady
quiz.explanation: The fainting lady holds the gown and pearls on her knees.

facts.text: The painting was thought lost for about 45 years before being found rolled up in 1973.
facts.explanation: It was written off after the 1928 flood and rediscovered by a curator.

facts.text: Delaroche shows the executioner as a cruel, grinning brute.
facts.explanation: He waits with lowered eyes, patient and almost sorry.

facts.text: The figures in the painting are roughly life-size.
facts.explanation: The canvas measures about 2.5 by 3 meters.
